questions.question: What is the WHERE clause in SQL and how does it filter rows?
questions.title: WHERE Clause in SQL — Filtering Rows
questions.direct_answer: **WHERE** filters rows from a table based on a condition. Only rows where the condition evaluates to TRUE are returned. It supports operators: =, <>, >, <, >=, <=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL, and logical AND/OR/NOT.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic WHERE clause syntax and common operators
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using = NULL instead of IS NULL, or misunderstanding AND/OR precedence
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention operator precedence (AND before OR) and that WHERE executes before GROUP BY and SELECT

sections.title: WHERE Clause Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- WHERE filters rows before any grouping or aggregation happens
- `<>` and `!=` both mean 'not equal' in SQL
- AND has higher precedence than OR — use parentheses to be explicit
- `WHERE col = NULL` never returns rows — use `IS NULL`
- WHERE cannot use column aliases from SELECT (SELECT runs after WHERE)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The WHERE clause filters rows in a SQL query — only rows where the condition is true are included in the result. It supports comparison operators like equals, greater than, less than, as well as BETWEEN for ranges, IN for multiple values, LIKE for pattern matching, and IS NULL for null checks. One important thing about AND and OR: AND has higher precedence than OR, so if you mix them use parentheses to make the logic explicit. Also, WHERE is processed before SELECT, so you cannot use column aliases defined in SELECT inside the WHERE clause.

Why does WHERE col = NULL not work?
What is the precedence of AND vs OR in SQL?

questions.question: How does the LIKE operator work in SQL?
questions.title: LIKE Operator in SQL — Pattern Matching
questions.direct_answer: **LIKE** performs pattern matching in WHERE clauses. `%` matches any sequence of characters (including empty), `_` matches exactly one character. Example: `WHERE name LIKE 'J%'` matches all names starting with J.

interviewer_intent.testing: LIKE operator syntax and wildcard behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing % (any characters) with _ (one character), or not knowing that leading % prevents index usage
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that LIKE '%java%' cannot use a B-tree index (full table scan), while LIKE 'java%' can use the index

sections.title: LIKE Pattern Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- `%` wildcard: matches zero or more characters
- `_` wildcard: matches exactly one character
- LIKE is case-insensitive in MySQL by default; case-sensitive in PostgreSQL
- Leading % (`LIKE '%text'`) forces a full table scan — cannot use index
- `NOT LIKE` excludes matching rows
- For complex pattern matching, use REGEXP/RLIKE in MySQL

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The LIKE operator in SQL is used for pattern matching in WHERE clauses. It has two wildcards: percent matches zero or more characters, and underscore matches exactly one character. So LIKE 'J%' matches any name starting with J, LIKE '%@gmail.com' matches email addresses ending in gmail.com, and LIKE 'J_va' would match 'Java' or 'Jova'. An important performance consideration: when you use a leading percent like LIKE percent-java-percent, SQL cannot use an index and must do a full table scan. But LIKE 'java%' with the percent at the end can still use an index because it's a prefix search.

followup_questions: What is the difference between % and _ in LIKE?
Why does LIKE '%text' cause a full table scan?
How is LIKE different from REGEXP in MySQL?

speakable_v2.cap: Percent for any sequence, underscore for one character — and never lead with percent if you care about index performance.

questions.question: What is the BETWEEN operator in SQL and when do you use it?
questions.title: BETWEEN Operator in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **BETWEEN** filters rows where a value falls within an inclusive range. `WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000` is equivalent to `WHERE salary >= 50000 AND salary <= 80000`. Both endpoints are included.

interviewer_intent.testing: BETWEEN syntax and inclusive range behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking BETWEEN is exclusive of endpoints — it is inclusive on both ends
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that BETWEEN works on dates and strings too, not just numbers

sections.title: BETWEEN Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends: `BETWEEN 10 AND 20` includes 10 and 20
- Works with numbers, dates, and strings
- `NOT BETWEEN` excludes the range
- Equivalent to: `col >= low AND col <= high`
- For date ranges, be careful with timestamps — BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31' misses the last day's records after midnight

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: BETWEEN is a shorthand for range filtering in SQL. It's inclusive on both ends — so WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000 includes employees with exactly 50000 or exactly 80000 salary. It's equivalent to writing salary greater than or equal to 50000 AND salary less than or equal to 80000. BETWEEN works with numbers, dates, and strings. One gotcha with dates: if you're filtering timestamp columns and use BETWEEN on just dates, records from the end date after midnight may be missed, so be careful about time components in date ranges.

followup_questions: Can BETWEEN be used with dates?
How would you filter rows outside a range?

speakable_v2.cap: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends and works on dates and strings too — watch out for timestamp precision at the upper bound.

questions.question: What is the IN operator in SQL and how is it different from OR?
questions.title: IN Operator in SQL vs Multiple OR Conditions
questions.direct_answer: **IN** checks if a value matches any value in a list. `WHERE dept IN ('IT', 'HR')` is equivalent to `WHERE dept = 'IT' OR dept = 'HR'` but cleaner. IN also works with subqueries to filter against a dynamic set.

interviewer_intent.testing: IN operator syntax including subquery usage
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that IN with a subquery is very powerful for filtering against dynamic sets
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that IN with NULL values can produce unexpected results, and compare IN vs EXISTS for subquery performance

sections.title: IN Operator Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- IN is cleaner than multiple OR conditions
- IN with subquery is powerful — dynamically filters based on another query
- `NOT IN` with NULL in the list: if the subquery returns any NULL, NOT IN returns no rows
- IN vs EXISTS: EXISTS is often faster for large subquery results (stops at first match)
- IN is case-insensitive for strings in MySQL (default collation)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The IN operator checks if a column value matches any value in a provided list. It's essentially a cleaner way to write multiple OR conditions. So WHERE department IN IT, HR, Finance is the same as writing department equals IT OR department equals HR OR department equals Finance. IN becomes especially powerful when combined with a subquery — for example, WHERE employee ID IN SELECT manager ID FROM departments, which filters employees who are managers. One important caveat: if you use NOT IN with a subquery and that subquery returns any NULL values, NOT IN will return no rows at all, which is a common gotcha.

followup_questions: What happens with NOT IN when the list contains NULL?
When would you use EXISTS instead of IN?
Can IN be used with a subquery?

beats.content: IN checks whether a column value matches any item in a list. WHERE department IN IT, HR, Finance is equivalent to three OR conditions joined together — just cleaner to read and easier to extend. IN also works with a subquery, letting you filter rows dynamically based on another query's results.

sharp edge: NOT IN with a subquery breaks silently if the subquery returns any NULL. Because NULL compared to anything is UNKNOWN, the NOT IN condition evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row and returns no results at all. Use NOT EXISTS instead when the subquery might include nulls.

speakable_v2.cap: Use IN for clean list matching and subqueries — but switch to NOT EXISTS when nulls might appear in the comparison set.

questions.question: What is the difference between AND and OR in SQL WHERE clause?
questions.title: AND vs OR Operator Precedence in SQL WHERE
questions.direct_answer: **AND** and **OR** combine multiple conditions. AND requires ALL conditions to be true; OR requires at least ONE. AND has higher precedence than OR, so `a OR b AND c` is evaluated as `a OR (b AND c)`. Use parentheses to control precedence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Logical operator behavior and precedence in WHERE clauses
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that AND has higher precedence than OR, leading to incorrect filter logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example showing how missing parentheses changes query results

sections.title: AND vs OR Precedence
Key Points
sections.content:
- AND: all conditions must be true — more restrictive
- OR: at least one condition must be true — less restrictive
- Precedence: NOT > AND > OR
- Always use parentheses when mixing AND and OR to make intent clear
- Short-circuit evaluation: if first AND condition is false, second is not evaluated

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: AND and OR are logical operators for combining conditions in WHERE clauses. AND requires all conditions to be true, making the filter more restrictive. OR requires at least one condition to be true. The critical thing to remember is operator precedence: AND is evaluated before OR. So if you write WHERE department equals HR OR department equals IT AND salary greater than 60000, SQL evaluates it as HR OR open-paren IT AND salary greater than 60000 close-paren — which gives you all HR employees regardless of salary, plus IT employees with salary over 60000. If you wanted all HR and IT employees with salary over 60000, you'd need to wrap the OR in parentheses. I always recommend using parentheses when mixing AND and OR to make the intent explicit.

followup_questions: What is the operator precedence for NOT, AND, and OR?
How would you get employees from IT or HR with salary above 60000?
What is short-circuit evaluation in SQL?

beats.content: AND requires all conditions to be true — it makes your filter more restrictive. OR requires at least one condition to be true — it broadens the filter. The trap is operator precedence: AND is evaluated before OR, just like multiplication before addition in math.

candidates miss: this query looks like it filters both departments with the same salary threshold — but it does not. WHERE department equals HR OR department equals IT AND salary is greater than 60000. SQL reads this as HR, or any IT employee with salary over 60000. To get HR and IT employees both filtered by salary, you must wrap the OR in parentheses: WHERE open-paren department equals HR OR department equals IT close-paren AND salary greater than 60000.

Always use parentheses when mixing AND and OR — it makes intent explicit and prevents bugs

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
questions.title: WHERE vs HAVING in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **WHERE** filters individual rows before grouping; it cannot use aggregate functions. **HAVING** filters groups after GROUP BY; it can use aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM. WHERE is faster as it reduces rows before aggregation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of WHERE vs HAVING execution order
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting aggregate conditions in WHERE instead of HAVING
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain execution order and why WHERE is more efficient — it eliminates rows before the expensive aggregation step

sections.title: WHERE vs HAVING Example
sections.content:
-- WHERE: filter rows before grouping (salary > 30000)
-- HAVING: filter groups after (only depts with 5+ employees)
SELECT department, COUNT(*), AVG(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 30000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: WHERE and HAVING both filter data, but at different stages. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, and it cannot reference aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after the GROUP BY is applied, and it can use aggregate functions. A good example: if you want departments with more than 5 employees where individual salaries are above 30000, you'd put the salary condition in WHERE to filter rows first, then use HAVING COUNT star greater than 5 to filter the resulting groups. This is also more efficient because WHERE reduces the data set before the expensive GROUP BY and aggregation operations.

speakable_v2.hook: WHERE versus HAVING is one of the most-asked SQL interview questions — and the answer is all about when each one runs.

beats.content: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY is applied. The key consequence: WHERE cannot use aggregate functions like COUNT or SUM because those haven't been calculated yet. HAVING can, because it runs after aggregation.

A practical example: to find departments where all salaries are above 30000 and the department has at least 5 employees, put the salary condition in WHERE to cut rows early, then use HAVING COUNT star greater than or equal to 5 to filter the resulting groups. WHERE is also more efficient — it reduces the data set before the expensive aggregation step.

speakable_v2.cap: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after — put aggregate conditions in HAVING, not WHERE.
